topics.title: Propositions
notes: A proposition is a declarative sentence that is either true or false (not both).
True is written as T or 1, false as F or 0. Propositional variables are written as p, q, r, s.
Not propositions: questions (What time is it?), commands (Read this carefully), and sentences with unknown variables (x + y = z).

topics.title: Connectives: NOT, AND, OR, conditional, biconditional
notes: Negation ~p (NOT p): true when p is false.
Conjunction p ∧ q (AND): true only when both p and q are true.
Disjunction p ∨ q (OR): false only when both p and q are false.
Conditional p → q (if p then q): false only when p is true and q is false. p is the hypothesis, q is the conclusion.
Biconditional p ↔ q (p if and only if q): true when p and q have the same truth value.

topics.title: Converse, inverse and contrapositive
notes: For p → q: converse is q → p, inverse is ~p → ~q, contrapositive is ~q → ~p.
A conditional and its contrapositive always have the same truth value. The converse and the inverse are equivalent to each other, but not to the original statement.

topics.title: Precedence, tautology and contradiction
notes: Precedence (highest first): brackets, ~ (NOT), ∧ (AND), ∨ (OR), → (if then), ↔ (if and only if).
Tautology: a proposition that is always true. Example: p ∨ ~p.
Contradiction: a proposition that is always false. Example: p ∧ ~p.

topics.title: Truth tables
notes: A truth table lists all combinations of the variables. With n variables there are 2^n rows (2 variables: 4 rows, 3 variables: 8 rows).
Build the table column by column: first the simple parts (~p, p ∨ q), then the bigger expression. Use the final column for the answer.
Use the precedence rules and brackets to decide which column to compute first.

topics.title: Logical implication and equivalence
notes: Logical implication A ⇒ B: the statement A → B is a tautology.
Logical equivalence A ⇔ B (or A ≡ B): the statement A ↔ B is a tautology. Equivalent statements have identical truth tables.
To prove equivalence, make the truth tables of both sides and compare the final columns.

topics.title: Laws of propositional algebra
notes: Commutative: p ∨ q ≡ q ∨ p and p ∧ q ≡ q ∧ p.
Associative: p ∨ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∨ q) ∨ r and p ∧ (q ∧ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∧ r.
Distributive: p ∨ (q ∧ r) ≡ (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ r) and p ∧ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r).
De Morgan: ~(p ∨ q) ≡ ~p ∧ ~q and ~(p ∧ q) ≡ ~p ∨ ~q.

short.q: Which of these is a proposition: '2 is an even integer' or 'x + y = z'? Give a reason.
short.answer: '2 is an even integer' is a proposition (it is true). 'x + y = z' is not, because its truth value depends on the values of x, y, z.

short.q: Write the truth table of p ∧ q.
Write the converse, inverse and contrapositive of: 'If it is raining, then the ground is wet.'
short.answer: Converse: If the ground is wet, then it is raining. Inverse: If it is not raining, then the ground is not wet. Contrapositive: If the ground is not wet, then it is not raining.

short.q: Define tautology and contradiction with one example each.
short.answer: Tautology is always true, e.g. p ∨ ~p. Contradiction is always false, e.g. p ∧ ~p.

short.q: Is p ∨ ~p a tautology? Justify with a truth table.
short.answer: Yes. When p=0, ~p=1 so p ∨ ~p = 1. When p=1, p ∨ ~p = 1. The result is always true, so it is a tautology.

short.q: For A: p → q and B: ~q → ~p, show that A ⇔ B using a truth table.
short.answer: Both A and B have the same truth values in all 4 rows (T,F,T,T), so A ↔ B is a tautology. Hence A ≡ B and A ⇒ B.
